summary:
Putrajaya is a federal territory of Malaysia and the country's administrative capital. It stands under the national framework: Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at federal level, and the territory's own Sharia code adds a second layer that reaches Muslims only.

Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Sharia enactments in all 13 states and in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only. State Islamic religious departments enforce them, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation has no domestic mechanism to align documents before travel.

Litigation has narrowed the Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. A High Court request to declare the cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional was denied, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public. Since the 2018 election, documented action includes an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested and an August raid on an LGBT venue that detained twenty men; a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.

In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister stated that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Putrajaya Sharia cross-dressing offence does not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and in November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres, indicating state sponsorship of identity-change programmes alongside criminal enforcement.

The constitutional position has shifted on federalism grounds rather than on rights grounds. The Federal Court's February 2021 ruling on Selangor's section 28 and its February 2024 ruling on 16 Kelantan provisions turned on which level of government may legislate, and left the federal Penal Code provisions untouched.

A constitutional challenge remained pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects at federal level, and LGBT events and media content are censored. Several governments in the region retain comparable colonial-era sodomy provisions, though few combine them with a territorially widespread cross-dressing offence.
localsOnly:
Malaysian Muslims live under two enforceable layers: the federal Penal Code and their state or territory Sharia enactment, which for cross-dressing carries up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men.

The Sharia enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dressing, so the scope of the offence is set by enforcement practice rather than statute.

No legal gender-recognition procedure exists, which affects identity documents, employment and interaction with authorities for residents as well as visitors.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 for a report on conversion practices, discrimination and violence published on 10 August 2022. Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had been attended by at least 1,733 people as of June 2021.

Justice For Sisters provides bail support and legal aid to people detained in raids. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in under two months, in a case documented under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself", which records police mistreatment and impunity.

Residents have no statutory protection: there is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Putrajaya-specific enforcement case is documented in the available sources; the raids, arrests and killings cited here occurred in other Malaysian states and federal territories and are used to indicate the national pattern a visitor would stand under.

The sources do not state the precise text or penalty of Putrajaya's own cross-dressing provision, nor whether it departs from the model wording used elsewhere in Malaysia; the penalties given are those recorded for Sharia cross-dressing offences generally.

How often foreign visitors are stopped on presentation-based grounds outside raids is not quantified in the sources, and no statistical breakdown of arrests by nationality beyond the 31 foreign nationals held during the November 2025 raid is available.

The sources do not specify which authority would handle a gender-recognition application in the absence of a recorded legal procedure, or the current status of the constitutional challenge pending as of late 2014.
